rows.verified: Employers must manage ionising-radiation risks to protect workers and members of the public.
Ionising radiation includes X-rays, gamma rays and radiation from radioactive sources and naturally occurring sources such as radon.
Low-risk ionising-radiation work may require notification, medium-risk work registration and high-risk work consent.
IRR17 requires exposure to be kept as low as reasonably practicable and below specified dose limits.
Engineering controls and design features should be used before relying on safe systems or personal protective equipment.
Workplaces with annual average radon concentrations above 300 Bq per cubic metre must notify HSE.
Certain high-risk ionising-radiation practices require a safety assessment and HSE consent before work starts.
Industrial-radiography incidents are associated with poor planning, inadequate source shielding and inadequate systems of work.
Ionising-radiation risk depends on source type, activity, energy, distance, shielding, duration, work practice, monitoring and individual dose history.
HSE ionising-radiation evidence is source-, practice-, workplace-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health probability.
HSE non-ionising-radiation guidance covers optical radiation and electromagnetic fields.
Electromagnetic fields are produced whenever electrical or electronic equipment is used.
Employers must assess and manage workplace EMF risks and provide necessary information and training.
Employers must assess employee EMF exposure against action levels and exposure-limit values.
EMF controls must consider workers at particular risk, including people with implanted or body-worn medical devices.
EMF effects covered by the regulations include sensory effects, shocks, nerve stimulation, heating and indirect device interference.
The artificial-optical-radiation regulations protect workers from hazardous sources of artificial optical radiation.
Even where an EMF exposure-limit exemption applies, exposure must remain as low as reasonably practicable and workers must be protected.
Non-ionising-radiation risk depends on frequency, intensity, distance, duration, equipment, shielding, worker susceptibility and implanted devices.
HSE non-ionising-radiation evidence is source-, frequency-, equipment-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health probability.
